title: “Sensual desire, monks, is an obscuration, a hindrance, a covering of the mind, debilitating to wisdom. Ill-will, monks … sloth and torpor … restlessness and…
content: “Sensual desire, monks, is an obscuration, a hindrance, a covering of the mind, debilitating to wisdom. Ill-will, monks … sloth and torpor … restlessness and remorse … doubt is an obscuration, a hindrance, a covering of the mind, debilitating to wisdom. These, monks, are the five obscurations, hindrances, coverings of the mind, debilitating to wisdom.”

title: Those who are intoxicated with states, Bewildered and confused, Led astray into wrong courses, Wandering amidst various views — They sleep on and on, They…
content:
Those who are intoxicated with states,
Bewildered and confused,
Led astray into wrong courses,
Wandering amidst various views —
They sleep on and on,
They do not wake up.
Now indeed the time has come
For them to awaken.

(The Blessed One):
Those who are not intoxicated with states,
Not bewildered or confused,
Not led astray into wrong courses,
Wandering amidst various views —
They have attained perfect enlightenment,
They have fully understood.
On the uneven path,
They walk evenly.

title: “Monks, there are these three elements of escape. What three? The escape from sensual pleasures — that is renunciation. The escape from form — that…
content:
“Monks, there are these three elements of escape. What three? The escape from sensual pleasures — that is renunciation. The escape from form — that is the formless. And as to whatever has come to be, is conditioned, dependently arisen, its escape is its cessation. These, monks, are the three elements of escape.

Knowing the escape from sensual pleasures,
And transcending all forms,
Always ardent, calming all conditioned things —
That monk sees rightly.

From that, being thus liberated,
He perfects direct knowledge,
Dwells at peace, in that very life,
That sage has crossed beyond all yokes.”

title: Do not pursue the past, Do not long for the future. The past is left behind, The future has not yet come. Only the present…
content:
Do not pursue the past,
Do not long for the future.
The past is left behind,
The future has not yet come.
Only the present Dhamma —
See it clearly here and now.
Unmoved, unshaken —
Knowing this, cultivate it.
Make an effort today —
Who knows death tomorrow?
No one can negotiate
With the great army of Death.
Living thus ardently,
Both day and night untiring —
That is called the Sage of the One Night,
The peaceful, the calm.

title: “Contact, monks, is one extreme. The origination of contact is the second extreme. The cessation of contact is the middle. Craving is the weaver; for…
content:
“Contact, monks, is one extreme. The origination of contact is the second extreme. The cessation of contact is the middle. Craving is the weaver; for craving weaves one to be reborn in this or that state of existence. Thus, monks, a monk directly knows what should be directly known, fully understands what should be fully understood. By directly knowing what should be directly known and fully understanding what should be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering here and now.
Knowing both extremes,
Not stained in the middle,
I call that great person,
He has surpassed the weaver.”

title: “One without craving, wise, Without doubt, Having merged into the deathless — Him I call a brahmin.” “One who in this world Is not stained…
content:
“One without craving, wise,
Without doubt,
Having merged into the deathless —
Him I call a brahmin.”

“One who in this world
Is not stained by good and evil,
Griefless, stainless, pure —
Him I call a brahmin.”

“Like the moon, stainless,
Clear, pure, calm,
With craving for existence destroyed —
Him I call a brahmin.”

“Who has crossed this dangerous path,
Saṃsāra and delusion,
Gone to the further shore,
Meditative, without sensual desire, without doubt,
Not clinging, at peace —
Him I call a brahmin.”

title: “Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon, that becomes the inclination of his mind. Monks, if a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon…
content: “Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon, that becomes the inclination of his mind. Monks, if a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon sensual thoughts, he has abandoned thoughts of renunciation. When his mind has become heavy with sensual thoughts, his mind inclines to sensual thoughts. Monks, if a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of ill-will … thoughts of harmfulness, he has abandoned thoughts of non-harmfulness. When his mind has become heavy with harmful thoughts, his mind inclines to harmful thoughts.”

title: “Monks, one who dwells seeing danger in things that are fetters — greed is abandoned, hatred is abandoned, delusion is abandoned. Because greed, hatred, and…
content: “Monks, one who dwells seeing danger in things that are fetters — greed is abandoned, hatred is abandoned, delusion is abandoned. Because greed, hatred, and delusion are abandoned, he is freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is freed from suffering.”

title: “Monks, this body is subject to destruction, consciousness is subject to vanishing, all attachments are impermanent, suffering, subject to change. Knowing the body’s destruction, And…
content:
“Monks, this body is subject to destruction, consciousness is subject to vanishing, all attachments are impermanent, suffering, subject to change.

Knowing the body’s destruction,
And that consciousness must vanish,
Seeing the peril in attachments,
Understanding birth and death —

Having attained the supreme peace,
The mind is well-developed,
He simply bides his time.”

title: “Monks, if wanderers of other sects ask you: ‘For what purpose, friends, is the holy life lived under the ascetic Gotama?’ — being asked thus,…
content: “Monks, if wanderers of other sects ask you: ‘For what purpose, friends, is the holy life lived under the ascetic Gotama?’ — being asked thus, monks, you should answer them: ‘For the purpose of the destruction of greed, friends, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.’ Then, monks, if they ask: ‘Is there, friends, a path, a way for the destruction of greed?’ — being asked thus, you should answer: ‘There is a path, a way for the destruction of greed.’ And what, monks, is that path, that way? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view … right concentration. This, monks, is the path, the way for the destruction of greed. Being asked thus, monks, you should answer them in that way.”
